1.x: “At the same time..”: This phrase tethers the dispute directly to the events of Mt 17. Jesus had just singled Peter out by paying the Temple tax only for himself and Peter (Mt 17:27). Prior to that, Peter, James, and John were selected to witness the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1). “..Who is the greatest...": The disciples are not asking an abstract theological question. They are looking for a hierarchy. Seeing Peter receive special tasks and mentions has triggered a competitive spirit among the twelve. They want Jesus to explicitly lay down the internal ranking of his cabinet. Matthew sanitizes the scene slightly by having the disciples ask Jesus directly. However, the parallel accounts in Mark 9 and Luke 9 reveal the ugly reality: the disciples had been fiercely arguing about this behind Jesus’ back walking down the road. “What was it that ye disputed among yourselves by the way? But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest." (Mk 9:33-34 KJV) - in Mark’s account, Jesus has to draw the confession out of them. They were arguing about their own ranking on the road and were too embarrassed to admit it when Jesus first asked. "Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." (Lk 9:46 KJV) - This is Luke’s account. The word “reasoning” (dialogismos in Greek) implies an internal, argumentative debate. They were actively measuring themselves against one another. This text serves as a strong historical and textual argument against the doctrine of Petrine Primacy (the belief that Jesus gave primacy to Peter the moment he gave him the keys of heaven in Mt 16:18-19) because: (1) The disciples clearly didn’t know Peter was the leader; if Jesus had clearly and definitively appointed Peter as the supreme head of the apostles just two chapters earlier (Mt 16), the debate in Mt 18 would be completely impossible. If Peter’s primacy was an established fact, the question of “Who is the greatest?” was already answered. The very fact that the disciples are arguing about who is the greatest proves that none of them (including Peter) understood Jesus’ words in Mt 16 as giving Peter a higher structural rank or permanent supremacy over the rest. (2) Jesus DOES NOT ANSWER: “Peter is the greatest.” When explicitly asked the question, “Who is the greatest?”, Jesus has the perfect opportunity to confirm Peter’s rank. He could have easily said: “Have you forgotten? I gave Simon the keys.” Instead, Jesus completely subverts the paradigm of structural hierarchy. In verses 2-4, Jesus defines greatness not by ecclesiastical office, titles, or keys, but by relative lowliness, dependence, and humility. (3) The “Keys” and Authority were given to ALL THE DISCIPLES. While Peter was addressed individually in Mt 16, Jesus expands this exact same authority to the entire group just a few verses later in Mt 18:18. In conclusion: Peter was often the spokesperson of the group because of his bold personality, but he held no unique corporate monopoly on authority. The keys of binding(rabbinic language for “prohibiting”) and loosing(rabbinic language for “permitting”) belonged to the entire apostolic body. In the Kingdom of Heaven, authority is collective, and true greatness is found in the willingness to serve, not the right to rule.

2.x: “Jesus called a little child”: The Greek word used here is paidion, which denotes a very young child, a toddler, or even an infant. “..and set him in the midst of them”: The disciples were looking up toward thrones of power and hierarchy. Jesus forces them to look down at a small child who occupied the absolute lowest rung of the social ladder in 1st-century Roman and Jewish society.

3.x: “..Except ye be converted..”: The Greek word for converted in strepho, meaning “to turn around” or “to reverse direction.” He tells the competitive disciples that they are walking in the wrong direction. They are chasing status: they need a total about-face (a military 180-degree turn). “..and become as little children..” Jesus establishes the young child as the ultimate model to follow. “..ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven”: Without this specific child-like transformation, entrance into the Kingdom is completely barred. To understand why a child is the model, we have to look at WHAT THE TODDLER LACKS, RATHER THAN WHAT THEY POSSESS. Jesus is not romanticizing children as morally perfect or sinless being (any parent knows children display selfishness early). Rather, he is highlighting their relational status of: (1) Absolute dependency to the Father: A little child cannot feed, clothe, protect, or sustain itself. It survives entirely on the provision of a parent. To enter the Kingdom, a person must abandon the illusion of self-sufficiency and depend entirely on God. (2) Total lack of status: A toddler has no resumes, no titles, no social leverage, and no achievements to boast of. They do not earn their place in the family; they receive it as a gift. (3) Trust and humility: Children naturally trust their caretakers implicitly. They do not suffer from the calculated pride, political maneuvering, and rank-seeking that the disciples were displaying in verse 1. This verse provides a profound foundation for the doctrine of child salvation (the belief that young children who die in infancy go to heaven automatically, without the aid of water baptism, confirmation, or any other ritual) because: (1) You cannot look to a model that is lost: Jesus commands adult disciples to change and become like little children to enter heaven. If little children themselves are spiritually lost, condemned, or outside of God’s grace prior to receiving a sacrament, Jesus’ analogy collapses. He would be telling his disciples to model themselves after those who are excluded from the Kingdom. By establishing the child as the benchmark for entrance, Jesus implies that THE CHILD IS ALREADY SECURE IN THE KINGDOM. (2) The Kingdom ALREADY BELONGS TO THEM: This is reinforced in the parallel passage of Matthew 19:14 (and Luke 18:16), where Jesus says: "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven." (KJV). Jesus DOES NOT say the Kingdom WILL belong to them once they are baptized; he states objectively that the Kingdom ALREADY BELONGS to little children. (3) Grace prior to Law and Sacraments: Scripturally, sin is imputed where there is knowledge of the Law (Rom 3:20; 4:15; 5:13; 7:7-9; Jn 15:22; Jms 4:17; Lk 12:47-48; Acts 17:30; 1 Tim 1:13). Little children do not possess the cognitive capacity to understand that Law, to willfully rebel against God, or to exercise saving faith. Because they lack the capacity to reject God’s grace, they are covered under the atonement of Christ until they reach moral accountability. Therefore, CHILDREN DO NOT NEED A PRIEST, A SACRAMENT, OR A RITUAL WATER BAPTISM TO CLEANSE THEM INTO SAFETY; they are already safely held by the character of the King, who points to them as the very definition of what His kingdom looks like.

Infant baptism expanded gradually early, but it is not original nor apostolic teaching. In the first and second century, Christian baptism is always described alongside repentance, faith, confession, fasting, and instruction - things associated with converts old enough to respond personally (for example Acts 2:38;8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; or the Didache, and early Christian writers like Justin Martyr & Tertullian). By the late second and third centuries, infant baptism began appearing due to very high infant mortality. Because many children died very young, Christian parents increasingly feared a child dying before baptism. Tertullian (200AC) is especially noteworthy because he argues AGAINST baptizing infants too early and urges delay. His objection itself shows the practice already existed in some communities but was not yet uncontested. As teaching about inherited sin from Adam developed more explicitly (especially through Augustine of Hippo in the late fourth and early fifth centuries) infant baptism became much more widespread and urgent in the West. Augustine argued that infants are born bearing original sin and therefore need baptism for remission of sin. This changed the pastoral stakes dramatically: baptism was no longer only initiation into the church but increasingly viewed as necessary to cleanse even newborn infants. Over time this accelerated the normalization of baptizing babies shortly after birth. The theology around unbaptized infants also shifted significantly. In Augustine’s time, the dominant concern was that unbaptized infants, lacking baptism, could not enter the kingdom of heaven and were therefore excluded from salvation (though Augustine considered their eternal punishment the “mildest”). Medieval Western theology later softened this with the idea of LIMBO (limbus infantium): unbaptized infants were thought neither to suffer the punishment of hell nor enjoy the beatific vision, but to exist in a state of natural happiness without heaven. Limbo became common teaching in medieval Catholic theology but was never formally defined as dogma. In recent Catholic teaching, especially reflected in the Catholic Church’s Catechism and 2007 document of the International Theological Commission, the emphasis shifted again: the church entrusts unbaptized infants to the mercy of God and expresses hope that God may save them, without defining exactly how. THE MODE OF BAPTISM CHANGED TOO. Early Christian baptism was done by immersion (something attested archaeologically and in the texts like the Didache, which prefers “living water” and pouring only as an alternative when enough water is not available. INFANT BAPTISM WAS LIKEWISE ORIGINALLY BY IMMERSION, including triple immersion in both East and West (one immersion per name of the Trinity). Over time, especially in the medieval Latin West, affusion (pouring) became increasingly common for practical reasons such as cold climate, church architecture, and the ease of baptizing fragile newborns. By the high Middle Ages and especially later medieval Italy (13th century), pouring water over an infant’s head became the ordinary Western practice replacing immersion. Sprinkling (aspersion) also existed, though historically pouring became more standard before mere sprinkling did. Meanwhile, Eastern churches generally retained infant immersion and still often practice it today. In conclusion, INFANT BAPTISM IS NOT APOSTOLIC TEACHING. Apostolic teaching is what Peter said on his very first time preaching the gospel: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized(baptizo: which means “to immerse”) every one of you IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST (which is the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Isa 9:6) for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” (Acts 2:38 KJV). Then verse 39, the very next verse says: “For the PROMISE is unto you, AND TO YOUR CHILDREN, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” Catholics ignore the fact that baptism means “immersion” and that it’s to be done “in the name of Jesus” & instead teach that “the promise” refers to baptism, hence, children and babies need to be baptized as well, since the promise is for them. But the Bible teaches that “the promise” is the Holy Spirit baptism, not water baptism. Literally, just a few verses before it states what the promise is: “that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I WILL POUR OUT OF MY SPIRIT UPON ALL FLESH: AND YOUR SONS AND YOUR DAUGHTERS shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams” (Acts 2:17 KJV). This is why Jesus told the disciples to not leave Jerusalem until “His Promise” of Holy Spirit baptism arrives: “And, behold, I send THE PROMISE of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high” (Lk 24:49 KJV). This “promise” is fulfilled in Acts 2:1-3, when people receive Holy Spirit baptism and begin speaking in tongues. This is where the Church of Christ begins.

4.x: Jesus directly answers the disciples’ original question from verse 1 (“Who is the greatest?”). In God’s economy, status is inverted. Greatness is not achieved by climbing over others or asserting authority; it is achieved by consciously lowering oneself. “..as this little child..”: A young child does not try to be humble; they simply ARE low in status. They have no social power, no wealth, and no legal standing in the ancient world. To humble oneself like a child means to intentionally relinquish the pursuit of rank, titles, and self-importance to depend 100% on your Father. The person who is most content with being unnoticed, dependent, and low on earth is considered the highest ranking in the eyes of God.

5.x: “whose shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me”: to “receive” means to welcome, care for, validate, and show hospitality to. In this context, “little child” pulls double duty: it applies literally to young children, but also metaphorically to “little ones in the faith”, believers who are weak, unimportant, or lack social status. Jesus says that how you treat the lowest, most vulnerable members of the community is exactly how we treat him. If you welcome someone who can offer you absolutely nothing in return (like a child), you are welcoming Christ himself.

6.x: “But whose shall offend…”: The Greek word for “offend” is skandalizo, wihch means to place a stumbling block in someone’s path, to entrap the, or to cause them to sin and fall away from the faith. “...one of these little ones which believe in me..”: Notice Jesus explicitly shifts the definition here. He specifies “little ones WHICH BELIEVE IN ME.” He is talking about young, fragile, or simple believers whose faith can be easily crushed or misled by the arrogance, bad examples, or false teachings of religious leaders. “..it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck..”: The Greek word for millstone is “mylos onikos,” which literally means as “ass-millstone.” This was not the small hand-millstone used by women in the kitchen, but a massive, heavy stone pulled by a donkey to grind grain. “.. and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea”: Drowning was a terrifying execution method used by the Romans, Greeks, and Syrians, but it was not a legal Jewish punishment. To Jews, dying at sea and being denied a proper burial was viewed as a horrific, cursed, fate. Jesus is using extreme hyperbole to make a point: It is better to suffer a brutal, violent, premature physical death than to face God’s judgement for destroying the faith of a vulnerable believer.

7.x: The disciples started this chapter arguing about their own prestige. Jesus ends this section by telling them that their reckless ambition doesn’t just keep them out of greatness, it actually threatens to turn them into stumbling blocks (skandalon) that could ruin simpler believers, putting the disciples themselves in danger of absolute fiercest judgements of God. “..for it must needs be that offences come..”: In a broken, fallen world populated by flawed human beings, temptation and moral traps are an inevitable reality. They cannot be completely avoided. “..but woe to that man by whom the offence cometh!”: Even though sin is inevitable in the grand scheme, individual responsibility is not erased. The person who chooses to create the trap, mislead the innocent, or act as the agent of temptation bears full, terrifying accountability before God.

8.x: “if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off..”: Jesus IS NOT advocating for physical self-mutilation (amputating a hand doesn’t stop the heart from lusting or envying). He is using drastic hyperbole to illustrate the severity of sin. The hand represents what we do or hold onto; the foot represents where we go. If an association, a habit, a career, or a possession is consistently trapping you in sin, it must be severed immediately. “...it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed..”: The word “halt” means limping or crippled; “mained” means missing a limb. Jesus presents a stark spiritual reality: It is infinitely better to live a restricted, disciplined life on earth (missing out on certain pleasures, wealth, or worldly experiences) and secure eternal life.

9.x: “if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out..”: The eye represents our desires, our gaze, and how we perceive the world (the “lust of the eyes”). It is the entry point for many temptations. Plucking it out means aggressively shifting your focus away from toxic, sinful influences. “..it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than … cast into hell”: The word Jesus uses here for hell is Gehenna. This was a literal place outside Jerusalem (the Valley of Hinnom) where garbage, animal carcasses, and the bodies of executed criminals were burned in a continuous fire. It served as the ultimate visual metaphor for eternal, agonizing separation from God (2 Thess 1:8-9). Applying this to the apostles that were just fighting for rank, Jesus’ lesson is that if the apostles kept feeding their desire for power, rank, and supremacy, those desires would become the very “hands, feet, and eyes” that would trip them up and throw them into Gehenna. Jesus demands a ruthless, surgical removal of anything (even things as dear to us as a right hand or an eye) that threatens our humility and our salvation.

In medieval Latin Roman Christianity, verses like Mt 18:8-9 (“if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off..”) were sometimes read metaphorically to defend removing dangerous corruption from the body of the church. The logic was: if a diseased limb threatens the body, it may need to be cut off to save the whole. “Heretics” (anyone who rejected Catholic doctrines) were portrayed as infecting the body of Christ, the Church, with false teaching, so eliminating heresy was framed as preserving the spiritual health of the “faithful.” The stronger biblical text most often cited, however, was Luke 14:23: “Compel them to come in..” Augustine of Hippo famously used this against the Donatists in North Africa. Earliest in life he opposed coercion, but later he argued the State could pressure heretics back into the church “for their correction,” comparing it to a loving father disciplining a child. That became enormously influential. Another common passage was Deuteronomy 13, where Israel is commanded to purge false prophets who lead people away from God. Medieval theologians saw Christian society as a continuation of sacred Israel in some sense, so civil rulers were urged to punish “heresy” as ancient Israel punished idolatry. By the high Middle Ages (13th century), theologians like Thomas Aquinas argued this explicitly. In the Summa Theologiae (11-11, q.11, a.3), Aquinas says if counterfeiters are put to death for corrupting temporal goods, then heretics (who corrupt the faith, a spiritual good) could be punished even more severly after ecclesiastical condemnation. The Church itself generally did not carry out executions directly; it condemned or excommunicated the person and handed them over to secular authority, who imposed penalties including imprisonment or execution, often by burning. But in practice, it was the church that coerced the State to carry out the executions with “infallible” bulls like Unam Sanctam and Council canons like Canon 3 “On Heretics” from the Fourth Lateran Council that threatened secular authorities with excommunication from the Church (since they taught you needed to be part of the Church to be saved, excommunication meant hell) for failing to purge the heresy identified by the Church. All of this, of course, contradicted the example of Jesus, who rebuked violence in matters of faith. For example Mt 13:28-30, where he says to let the wheat and the tares grow together; or Luke 9:54-56, where he rebukes the disciples for wanting to call down fire on the Samaritans.

10.x: “despise not”: to “despise” (kataphroneo) means to look down on, think little of, underestimate, or disregard as worthless. “...one of these little ones..”: These “little ones” includes literal children, but primarily refers to young, weak, simple, or socially insignificant believers: the people whom high-minded religious leaders are most likely to overlook or push aside. “..their angels..”: Jesus notes that these insignificant believers have “their angels” assigned to them or operating on their behalf in the spiritual realm. “..do always behold the face of my Father..”: In ancient Near Eastern courts, only the highest-ranking officials, ministers, and favorites of the king were granted direct, continuous access to look upon the king’s face (see 1 Kings 10:8; Esther 1:14). Jesus is using this royal imagery to make a staggering point: The angels assigned to watch over the lowliest believers are not low-ranking servants kept outside the gates. They have immediate, VIP access to the presence of God the Father. Hence, The man Jesus is saying: “How dare you look down on a poor, uneducated, or weak believer as if they are worthless? The highest-ranking, most glorious beings in heaven, who stand in the direct presence of Almighty God, consider it their highest honor to serve and protect them.” This verse also shows that: (1) Believers have angelic protection, which aligns perfectly with the OT depiction of angelic care, such as Psalm 91:11-12: "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone." (KJV). (2) The focus is on advocacy, not just protection. The common cultural view of a guardian angel is a floating entity that steps in to prevent car accidents or physical falls. While physical protection occurs in Scripture (Peter being broken out of prison in Acts 12). Jesus emphasizes a different role here: Advocacy and reporting. Because these angels “always behold the face” of the Father, they act as immediate witnesses. If you mistreat, abuse, or cause a weak believer to stumble, their assigned heavenly advocates have instant access to the Sovereign Judge of the universe to report the injustice. (3) It refutes the idea of “One Angel per person”: Scripture does not explicitly teach that every human being is assigned exactly one permanent, specific angel from birth to death. The NT model suggests that the angelic host works collectively on behalf of the church. As Heb 1:14 states: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?" (KJV).

11.x: This verse provides the ultimate theological foundation for why we must not despise or neglect weak believers (v.10). If the King of Glory left heaven to seek out and save things that were ruined, broken, and wandering, how can His disciples treat those same people with contempt or indifference?

12.x: Jesus drives home his warning against looking down on “little ones” by revealing the very heart of God. Through the Parable of the Lost Sheep, he illustrates that the Father is not a distant bureaucrat tracking percentages, but a passionate Shepherd who values the recovery of a single straying believer over the safety of the status quo. “..if a man have an hundred sheep, and one of them be gone astray…”: A flock of one hundred was a standard size for a moderately well-off family or a collective village flock. To lose one sheep is a 1% loss: economically manageable, but relationally unacceptable to a true shepherd. “..doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains…”: To human eyes, leaving 99 vulnerable sheep in the wilderness or hills to chase after one looks like bad business math. But the 99 are relatively secure together; the one that strayed is completely defenseless against predators, cliffs, and starvation. “...and seeketh that which is gone astray?”: The shepherd doesn’t wait for a sheep to find its own way back. HE INITIATES an active, exhausting, dangerous search in the rugged terrain (“the mountains”).

13.x: “And IF so be that he find it…”: The search is difficult, and the outcome is not guaranteed, highlighting the precarious situation of a believer who falls into sin or false teaching. “..verily I say unto you, he rejoiceth more of that sheep, than of the ninety and nine which went not astray”: This does not mean the shepherd loves the 99 less. Rather, it describes the psychology of joy over relief. You don’t throw a party for the children who are safely asleep in bed; you throw a party for the child who was missing in the woods and just walked through the front door.

14.x: “To perish” (apollumi) means to be ruined,destroyed, or eternally lost. Jesus applies the spiritual moral of the parable. God the Father (the divine Spirit) shares the exact same heart as the searching shepherd. Going back to how verse 1 started with the disciples arguing: “Who is the greatest? How do we build a hierarchy? Who gets the top seats?" By telling them this parable, Jesus effectively tells them: “You are focused on managing the 99 and establishing your rank over them. But my Father’s eyes are on the one that is missing.” True spiritual leadership does not look like sitting on a throne commanding the flock; it looks like stepping down into the mud, climbing mountains, and searching for the weak, broken, and straying “little ones” whom everyone else has forgotten.

Expressions like “our Father which is in heaven” are descriptions of God’s omnipresence and transcendence, rather than as evidence of a distinct person in the Godhead who is localized in a physical location separate from Jesus. God is an invisible, omnipresent Spirit, He cannot be physically confined to a literal throne room in the sky. As Solomon stated in 1 Kings 8:27: "the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee." Therefore, when the man Jesus says the Father is “in heaven,” He is usign human language to emphasize God’s transcendence, holiness, and supreme authority, contrasting it with the earthly, limited realm of humanity. It denotes where God’s glory is fully manifested, not a geographical location where one “person” of a Trinity resides while another “person” is on earth. The Son, as a real human being on earth, prayed, spoke of, and submitted to the divine Spirit (the Father), who also occupied the localized human body. However, As God, Jesus’ divine Spirit was still omnipresent, filling the universe and ruling from heaven. We can see this in John 3:13: "And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven, even the Son of man WHICH IS IN HEAVEN." (KJV) - this verse shows that while Jesus was standing on earth speaking to Nicodemus, his divine Spirit was simultaneously in heaven (this is the TR & MT reading, which consists of 97.6% of available manuscripts. The CT removes the “which is in heaven” part following the two oldest manuscripts which consists of 1.1% of available manuscripts). So when Jesus references “your Father which is in heaven,” he is not pointing the disciples to a second divine person in the sky. He is pointing them to the sovereign, omnipresent God who watches over the “little ones” via His heavenly host. If you could go to heaven and look at the Father, the only face you would see if the face of Jesus, because Jesus is the visible image of the invisible Father (Col 1:15). THE IDEA THAT GOD-THE-FATHER REMAINS IN HEAVEN, WHILE ONLY GOD-THE-SON COMES TO EARTH comes from Greek philosophy adopted by Trinitarians. Historically, there was a transformation of the biblical “Father” into the “God of the Philosophers,” a being characterized as completely ineffable (unknowable, beyond words) and IMPERSONAL. This shift occurred during the 2nd through 4th centuries with Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr who attempted to defend their faith to the educated Roman and Greek world. To do this, they translated the Hebrew concept of God into the language of Greek metaphysics (specially Platonism and Stoicism). The personal, relational Father was systematically realigned with the supreme abstract principle of the philosophers. The Biblical “Father” in the OT and the gospels was intensely personal. He speaks, experiences grief, covenants with people, and is described in anthropomorphic terms (having hands, eyes, and feet). Jesus emphasizes this personal intimacy by calling Him Abba (Father), a title of relational dependence. The Greek philosophers (like Plato, Aristotle, and later Plotinus) sought the ultimate, unchanging cause behind the universe, whom Plato called it The Good or The One. Aristotle called it the Unmoved Mover. To them, the Supreme Being had to be completely immutable (unchanging) and impassible (unable to feel emotion). If a being can change or feel emotion, it implies imperfection or vulnerability. Therefore, the ultimate god had to be a cold, static, abstract principle - utterly IMPERSONAL. When early Christian thinkers (like Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen) began writing to the Roman Emperor and Greek elites, they used Plato’s playbook. They wanted to prove that Christianity was not a “barbaric superstition” BUT THE HIGHEST PHILOSOPHY. The Greek philosophes argued that the true God is ineffable (beyond human language). The Christian Apologists adopted this completely. They began to argue that “Father” was not God’s actual name, but merely a functional title. Justin Martyr (2nd Century) wrote: "For God has no name given to Him... For names are given to mark and distinguish things... But no one was before God to give Him a name." God became the "Unbegotten, Ineffable, Immutable Source." The intimate Father of Jesus was recast as the ultimate, unknowable abstract baseline of existence. To satisfy the philosophers, Christian theologians also adopted the Greek concept of IMPASSIBILITY (the total absence of passion or emotion). If the Supreme God feels anger, sorrow, or pity, the Greeks argued He is weak and subject to external influences. Therefore, the Christian Apologists argued that when the Bible says God “grieves” or is “angry,” it is an accommodation to human language. In reality, God experiences absolutely no emotion. By stripping God of emotional responsiveness, He functionally became an impersonal force or static perfection. THIS PHILOSOPHICAL SYNTHESIS FORCED A STRUCTURAL SPLIT IN HOW CHRISTIANS VIEWED THE GODHEAD, paving the way for classic Logos Christology found in the Trinity: (1) The Supreme God / The Father (the Unknowable, Ineffable Spirit THAT CANNOT BE NAMED) → (2) The Logon / The Son (The Expressed Mind, Wisdom, Intermediary) → (3) The Material World (Creation, Humanity, History). Because the Father was now defined by Greek metaphysics as completely transcendent, invisible, and unable to touch matter or change, HE COULD NOT BE THE ONE WHO APPEARED TO MOSES IN THE BURNING BUSH, NOR COULD HE BE THE ONE WHO BECAME INCARNATE IN JESUS. The early Imperial Church fathers argued that the Father stays completely detached in the heavenly realm, while the Logos (the eternal Son) is the one who comes down, speaks to prophets, suffers, and acts. The Father became the static, impersonal “God of the Philosophers,” while the Son inherited all the personal, relational dynamics of the Biblical narrative. This historical shift is precisely what modern Oneness theologians (like David K. Bernard) and certain biblical historians critique. Oneness theology argues that this Greek philosophical invasion stripped God of His personal closeness, forcing a division into a “Trinity” where the Father is distant and only the Son is near. Oneness Christianity seeks to shatter this Greek concept of an ineffable, impersonal Father by asserting that the full, personal, emotional reality of the Father is not trapped in an abstract sky, but was fully manifested, visible, and touchable in the human face of Jesus Christ. This unnameable, ineffable, and impersonal God of the Greeks also influenced the Jews before the Christians, for they soon became afraid of even mentioning the tetragrammaton (YHWH) and replaced it with Kurios(LORD) instead. Due to this, when the LXX (Septuagint) was written, it was no longer prohibited to blaspheme the name of the LORD(YHWH), now by simply “naming” the name of YHWH you were condemned to stoning (Lev 24:16 LXX). For more examples that show how the translators of the LXX modified the Greek translation of the OT to make YHWH seem less personal and without a name, see: Lev 24:16; Ex 3:14; Hosea 11:9; Amos 9:6; Deut 32:8; Gen 2:4; 3:8-9; Psalm 23:1; etc.

15.x: “if thy brother shall trespass against thee”: This establishes that the offense is personal and direct between two individuals within the faith community (“brother”). It does not refer to public heresy or general layout of doctrine, but a private wrong. “Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone”: The first step is strictly private. Jesus commands the offended party to initiate the conversation quietly. This prevents gossip, protests the offender’s reputation, and minimizes defensiveness. “If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother”: If the offender acknowledges the fault and repents, the matter is completely resolved without escalating the issue. The ultimate goal is gaining back the broken relationship.

16.x: “But if he will not hear thee”: If private confrontation fails due to stubbornness or disagreement, the process escalates to step two. “Then take with thee one or two more”: The offended person brings a small, neutral group. These individuals are not a “jury” to gang up on the offender; they serve as objective observers. “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established”: Jesus directly quotes the Mosaic legal standard from Deut 19:15. The role of these witnesses is to verify the facts of the dispute, ensure the confrontation is handled justly, and witness whether the offender genuinely refuses to repent. God always follows this Law. Even in the man Jesus there were two witnesses: (1) the man Jesus (the Son) and (2) the divine Spirit (the Father), yet the two were one (Jn 10:30), a temple and visible image to the invisible Spirit. The truth of Christianity NEVER COMES FROM JUST ONE SOURCE: God presents His truth as polyphonic: many prophets, many apostles, many books, one coherent message of OT prophecies fulfilling in Jesus. While fake religions like Islam and Mormonism are centered on a single founding revelation and a single revelatory figure in isolation. Catholicism makes this same mistake, having a fallible man as the top and source of truth, rather than a collegiate of sources and apostles. Jesus did not give Peter any special authority that he did not give the rest of the apostles, as shown in the very next verses (v. 18), where the rest of the apostles are given the same keys of authority as Peter to “bind” and to “loose” doctrine.

17.x: “Tell it to the church”: If the small group consensus fails to bring about repentance, the matter is brought before the local assembly (ekklesia) of believers. “But if he neglect to hear the church”: This implies a formal, collective appeal from the local congregation urging the individual to make things right. “Let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican”: If the individual rejects the collective voice of the local assembly, their status changes. A “heathen” (Gentile) and a “publical” (tax collector) were outsiders to the Jewish community. In a NT context, this means the unrepentant person is treated as an unbeliever: excommunicated from the close fellowship of the assembly, though still a subject for evangelism and prayer. The ultimate goal is ALWAYS to save their soul, so even when they’re excommunicated, they’re separated for two reasons: (1) so a bad apple does not corrupt the other apples; & (2) “To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” (1 Cor 5:5 KJV) - so that Satan beats them up so badly that they will ultimately repent of their sins. Discipline is aimed at repentance, not cruelty for its own sake.

The Roman Catholic Church frequently points to v.17 (“tell it to the church”) as a proof text for the authority of the Catholic Papacy and the Magisterium. The argument claims that Christ was establishing a centralized, hierarchical institution centered in Rome with supreme judicial authority to settle disputes. From a strict historical, textual, and linguistic perspective, applying this passage to the modern ROman Catholic Church is an anachronism (something that is out of its proper time period, like a smart phone in a medieval movie). First, the Greek word translated as “church” is “ekklesia”. In the 1st-century Grego-Roman world, an ekklesia was simply a called-out assembly or a local congregation of citizens gathered for a specific purpose. For example, “ekklesia” referred to the congregation of Israel assembled in the wilderness (Acts 7:38). Jesus’ listeners in Mt 18 would have understood ekklesia to mean a local congregation or assembly of believers, not a global bureaucratic hierarchy spanning multiple continents under a single bishop. Second, Jesus outlines a swift, localized disciplinary process. “Tell it unto the church” occurs immediately after a private meeting with two or three witnesses fails. If the “Church” meant the global Roman Catholic institution, a local believer dealing with a personal trespass would have to escalate their private dispute to a localized diocese, an archbishop, a college of cardinals, or the Pope himself to get a ruling. The text assumes that the entire “church” being spoken to can hear the case and collectively speak back to the offender (“if he neglects to hear the church”). This is structurally possible only within a local body of believers who personally know the individuals involved. And thirdly, when Jesus spoke these words, the Roman Catholic Church (with its distinct structure of a Pope, Vatican, Cardinals, and Canon Law) did not exist. The setting is distinctly Jewish-Christian. Christ uses terms his disciples understood at that specific moment in history (“heathen man and a publican”, referencing Jewish cultural outsiders). The Church in Rome didn’t exist yet. Rome did not have a centralized, mono-episcopacy (a single ruling bishop) dominant over all other churches until CENTURIES later. NT churches were uniformly local assemblies overseen by pluralities of elders/pastors (Acts 12:23, Titus 1:5). So Jesus is not creating a vast legal hierarchy in Rome. He is giving a practical, local blueprint for church discipline. The “church” in this context is simply the local assembly of believers capable of meeting together, hearing a local dispute, and dealing with it directly.

18.x: This verse must be read in direct connection with the local assembly discipline process outlined in the preceding verses. “Verily I say unto you(plural)”: In the original Greek, the pronouns here shift explicitly. While Christ spoke to Peter individually in Mt 16:19 using singular pronouns (“thee” and “thou”), here in Mt 18:18 Jesus uses plural (ymin) for “you,” and plural verbs for “binding” and “loosing.” HE IS ADDRESSING THE ENTIRE GROUP OF DISCIPLES, and by extension, the local congregation. “Whateversoever ye shall bind.. Whatsoever ye shall loose”: In 1st-century Jewish legal and rabbinic language, to “bind” meant to forbid or declare unlawful, and to “loose” meant to permit or declare lawful. In the context of v.17 (church discipline), it specifically refers to the authority of judicial administrative “binding,” confirming that an unrepentant person is bound to their sin and excluded from fellowship, or “loosing” them from that judgement upon genuine repentance. “Shall be bound in heaven.. Shall be loosed in heaven”: A more precise rendering of the Greek future perfect passive verbs is “shall have been bound” and “shall have been loosed” (the more literal modern translations like the NASB or LSB translate it like that). The local church does not force Heaven’s hand or create new laws; rather, when a local assembly acts in accordance with Christ’s commands, they are merely ratifying on earth a judgement that has already been decreed in Heaven.

The Roman Catholic Church relies heavily on Matthew 16:19, where Jesus says individually to Peter: “And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou salt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven..” Catholic theology uses this to argue that Peter was uniquely granted absolute, infallible authority over the global Church, a supremacy passed down exclusively to the Popes of Rome. Matthew 18:18 completely dismantles the idea that this binding and losing authority belonged exclusively to Peter. In Mt 18:18, Jesus gives the exact same authority to bind and to loose to the rest of the apostles and the local assembly that he gave to Peter two chapters earlier. Peter was not given a unique judicial mechanism that the others lacked. Whatever administrative or disciplinary power Peter held, the other apostles and the local congregation held concurrently. Look closely at the chain of command Jesus builds in verses 15-17: (1) The offended individual; (2) Two or three witnesses; (3) The church (ekkelsia/ the local assembly). If Jesus intended for Peter (and his supposed successors) to be the unique, supreme, infallible head of the Church on earth, step four of this disciplinary process would logically be: “And if he neglect to hear the church, TELL IT UNTO PETER, THE CHIEF SHEPHERD.” Instead, the local assembly is the final court of appeal in the text. There is no higher earthly authority mentioned to override the decision of the local congregation when they are gathered in Christ’s name. Also, Jesus reinforces this collaborative, non-hierarchical authority in the very next verse: "Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven." (Mt 18:19) - the authority to represent Heaven’s Will on earth relies on the unified agreement (“if two of you shall agree”) of the disciples, not the solo, infallible ex-cathedra decree of a single bishop. So, while Peter was often the first to speak or act as a representative of the twelve (such as using the “keys of knowledge” to open the gospel to the Jews at Pentecost in Acts 2 and the Gentiles in Acts 10), Matthew 18:18 proves that the actual authority to govern, discipline, bind, and loose was shared equally among all the apostles and vested directly within the local body of believers.

19.x: Matthew 18:19-20 represents the conclusion of Jesus’ discourse on dealing with sin and conflict within the body of believers. While these verses are frequently quoted in isolation to describe corporate prayer meetings, their primary, immediate context is the legal and judicial ratification of church discipline. “Again I say unto you(plural)”: Jesus continues to speak to the collective group of disciples. The word “Again” links this thought directly back to the principles of binding and loosing in verse 18. “If two of you shall agree on earth”: The Greek word for “agree” is “symphōnēsōsin” from which we get the English word symphony. It means to sound together in perfect harmony. In a disciplinary context, it refers to at least two parties (matching the “two or three witnesses” of v. 16) coming to a harmonious, unified conclusion about a matter of sin, repentance, or restoration. “As touching any thing that they shall ask”: In context, this “asking” or requesting is not a blank check for material wealth or personal desires. It is a petition to God for wisdom, discernment, and confirmation regarding a JUDICIAL DECISION made by the assembly on earth. “It shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven”: When a local assembly operates in perfect, scriptural unity regarding church order, God promises to back their decision. The Father validates their harmonious earthly judgement because it aligns with His heavenly Will.

20.x: “For where two or three are gathered together”: Jesus intentionally sets the minimum number remarkably low. He matches the OT legal requirement for witnesses (“two or three”). This reinforces that a massive global hierarchy or a huge council is not required to execute Christ’s authority. Even the smallest local assembly meeting has full functional validity. “In my name”: To gather “in his name” means more than just repeating the phrase “in Jesus’ name” at the end of a prayer. It means gathering under his explicit authority, acting in accordance with his character, and strictly following his instructions (such as the steps laid out in verses 15-17). “There am I in the midst of them”: This is a profound statement of Christ’ omnipresence and divine authority. In Jewish rabbinic tradition, it was taught that if two or three sat together and studied the words of the Torah, the Shekinah (the divine presence of God) rested among them. Jesus claims that he is personally present to ratify, guide, and execute the decisions of the local assembly. By placing his personal presence and judicial backing with as few as “two or three,” Jesus completely bypasses any need for a singular, global, centralized earthly head (like a Pope). If a minute, local group of two or three believers gathers under the authority of Christ to resolve a conflict, Jesus himself is the final authority in the midst of them. No further hierarchical validation from an external earthly see is required to make their decision binding. But how can Jesus be present if he is supposed to be at “the right hand of God” after ascending into heaven? A Trinitarian may try to say that Jesus is now glorified, hence, he’s omnipresent. But then, who is helping us, omnipresent Jesus or the Holy Spirit? Who dwells in a believers’ heart, the Spirit of Jesus or the Holy Spirit? The answer is simple: THE DIVINE SPIRIT OF JESUS IS THE HOLY SPIRIT. Remember that “God is a Spirit” (Jn 4:24) and there is only “one Spirit” (Eph 4:4). Since God is an omnipresent Spirit, the terms “Holy Spirit,” “Spirit of God,” “Spirit of the Father,” and “Spirit of Christ” cannot refer to different spirits, or else there would be multiple divine spirits. The NT consistently uses the Spirit of Jesus interchangeably with the Holy Spirit. For example: (1) “After THE HOLY SPIRIT had prevented them from speaking the word in the province of Asia, they traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. And when they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but THE SPIRIT OF JESUS would not permit them..” (Acts 16:6-7 BSB, CT-based texts specify the “Spirit” is the “Spirit of Jesus”) - notice how the Holy Spirit is used interchangeably with the Spirit of Jesus. (2) “But ye are not in the flesh, but in THE SPIRIT, if so be that THE SPIRIT OF GOD dwell in you. Now if any man have not THE SPIRIT OF CHRIST, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV) - notice how the Spirit of God is used interchangeably with the Spirit of Christ; (3) “For I know that this shall turn to my salvation through your prayer, and the supply of THE SPIRIT OF JESUS CHRIST” (Phil 1:19 KJV); (3) “Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord(Jesus), the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord(Jesus) is THAT SPIRIT: and where THE SPIRIT of the Lord(Jesus) is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord(Jesus), are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by THE SPIRIT of the Lord(Jesus).” (2 Cor 3:16-18 KJV) - Paul consistently calls Jesus “the Lord”, and in v. 16 we see that turning to “the Lord” takes away the veil because it refers specifically to Jesus: “which vail is done away in Christ” (v.14). (4) Peter says that it was the “Spirit of Christ” which was in the OT prophets giving them prophecies (1 Peter 1:10-11), but the same Peter says it was the “Holy Spirit” that prophesied through the OT prophets (2 Peter 1:21), using the terms interchangeably. (5) John says Jesus will raise us up in the last day (Jn 6:40), yet Paul says it will be “the Spirit” (Rom 8:11). (6) Paul says that “the Spirit” raised Jesus from the dead (Rom 8:11), yet Jesus says he will raise himself up (Jn 2:19-21). (7) Jesus says he will ask the Father, who shall “give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever” (Jn 14:16 KJV), yet just two verses down he says: “I(Jesus) will not leave you comfortless: I(Jesus) will come to you” (Jn 14:18 KJV). In fact, this verse has the Trinity fulfilled in Jesus: “And I(the man Jesus) will ask the Father(the divine Spirit), and He(the divine Spirit) will give you another Advocate(the indwelling divine Spirit instead of through the man Jesus) to be with you forever — the Spirit of truth(the divine Spirit). The world cannot receive Him(the divine Spirit), because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him(fully dwelling in the man Jesus), for He abides with you(as the man Jesus) and will be in you(as the Holy Spirit). I(Jesus) will not leave you as orphans(aka “without a Father”); I(Jesus in Spirit mode) will come to you.” (Jn 14:16-18 BSB). (8) Jesus says that the Father will send “another Comforter, that he may abide with you FOR EVER” (Jn 14:16 KJV). Yet Jesus says during His Great Commission that he will be us “always, even unto the end of the world” (Mt 28:20 KJV). How? No longer as the man Jesus, but as the divine Spirit of Jesus (the Holy Spirit). (9) Jesus says to not worry about what we shall say, for the “Holy Spirit” will be talking through us (Mk 13:11), yet in Luke’s gospel, he says that Jesus himself will give us a mouth and wisdom to reply to our adversaries (Lk 21:15). (10) Since the divine Spirit of Jesus is the Holy Spirit, Jesus has to leave so that the Holy Spirit can indwell us: "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you." (Jn 16:7 KJV) - our counselor will no longer be the man Jesus, now it will be Jesus in Spirit mode as the Holy Spirit. If the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of Jesus were distinct persons, the NT would describe two divine entities living inside a Christian. Instead, scripture equates the indwelling of Christ with the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. So if the Spirit of Jesus is the same thing as the Holy Spirit, what is the name of the Holy Spirit? In John 14:26, Jesus states: "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send IN MY NAME (Jesus, YHWH-Saves)...” If the Holy Spirit comes in the name of Jesus, acts with the authority of Jesus, and performs the functions of Jesus within the believer, it is because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Jesus. The Holy Spirit is simply Jesus in another form (the spiritual form) so that He can dwell inside every believer simultaneously. Now you know what the name of the Father, Son, and Spirit is. For a deeper breakdown of the singular “name” of Matthew 28:19, see notes of that same verse.

The Bible is very explicit in that WE ARE TO DO ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING IN JESUS’ NAME, FOLLOWING HIS EXAMPLE AND COMMANDS, WHILE ALSO ORALLY INVOKING HIS NAME: “And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, CALLING ON THE NAME OF THE LORD(Jesus)” (Acts 22:16). Some of the examples explicitly listed are: (1) Pray in Jesus’ name (Jn 14:13-14; 16:23); (2) Gather together in Jesus’ name (Mt 18:20); (3) Baptize in Jesus’ name, which is the singular name of Mt 28:19 (see parallel passages of the Great Commission such as Mk 16:16-17 & Lk 24:46-47, where the name is obviously “Jesus” & “remission of sins” for Luke means repentance at water baptism, as he writes in Acts 2:38), where Jesus fulfills all three titles of Son, Counselor (Spirit), and Father (Isa 9:6). We see all his disciples obeying this command in Acts 2:38; 8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; where they ORALLY INVOKE Jesus’ name (Acts 22:16) & they rebaptize anyone who was baptized in any other way (Acts 19:3-5). Jesus is literally the only option, as it is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:10,12). (4) Preach in Jesus’ name (Lk 24:47; Acts 5:42); (5) Believe in Jesus’ name (1 Jn 3:23; Jn 1:12); (6) Receive forgiveness in Jesus’ name (Acts 10:43); (7) Heal the sick in Jesus’ name (Acts 3:6; Jms 5:14); (8) Cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Mk 16:17; Lk 10:17; Acts 16:18); (9) Perform miracles in Jesus’ name (Mt 7:22); (10) Teach in Jesus’ name (Acts 5:28); (11) Give thanks in Jesus’ name (Eph 5:20); (12) Do EVERYTHING in Jesus’ name: “And whatsoever ye do in word or dee, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him” (Col 3:17 KJV); (13) Welcome others in Jesus’ name (Mt 18:5); (14) Suffer persecution in Jesus’ name (Acts 5:41; Mt 5:11); (15) Be willing to leave things behind for Jesus’ name (Mt 19:29); (16) Hope in / Call upon the name of Jesus (Rom 10:13). HENCE, THE NT CONNECT JESUS’ NAME WITH: PRAYING, BAPTIZING, GATHERING, PREACHING, BELIEVING, RECEIVING FORGIVENESS, HEALING, CASTING OUT DEMONS, WORKING MIRACLES, TEACHING, GIVING THANKS, DOING ALL THINGS, WELCOMING OTHERS, SUFFERING FOR HIM, CALLING ON HIM FOR SALVATION, etc. Now, try to find ANYTHING in the Bible where something is done calling upon a vague, nameless Trinity. You won’t find absolutely anything since it was a clear human development rooted in confusion, it was never apostolic teaching.

21.x: Mt 18 is about Jesus instructing his disciples on community, humility, and restoration within the church. Peter’s question here stems directly from Christ’s previous instructions on how to handle a brother who sins against you (v.15-17). “Then came Peter to him..”: Peter seeks clarification on the limits of church discipline and personal patience. “...how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?”: Note the crucial phrasing: “AGAINST ME.” Peter is specifically asking about interpersonal offenses: personal wrongs, insults, or injuries committed by one individual against another within the community of faith. “..till seven times?”: In first-century rabbinic tradition (drawing from passages like Amos 1:3 KJV: “Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron”), it was commonly taught that a person was required to forgive an offender up to three times, but not more. By suggesting seven times, Peter likely thought he was being extraordinarily generous, doubling the requirement and adding one, matching the biblical number of completion or perfection.

22.x: “I say not unto thee, until seven times…”: Jesus immediately shatters Peter’s calculated boundary. By rejecting a literal cap, Jesus moves forgiveness out of the realm of legalistic accounting. “...but, until seventy times seven”: 70 x 7 = 490 times, however, Jesus is not doing literal math. He is alluding to the inverse of what Lamech did in Genesis 4:24, where he boasts about having avenged himself 70 x 7 times ("If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” [70 x 7]", BSB). Jesus replaces infinite vengeance with infinite forgiveness. The structural point is that by the time a person attempts to track 490 distinct offenses from the same brother, they will have entirely lost count, forcing them to abandon the ledger altogether and live in a constant state of grace.

Notice the forgiveness of sin that we can do is only sins committed against us, not sins committed against God’s Law. To understand the biblical boundaries of forgiveness, scripture distinguishes between two completely different types of forgiveness: interpersonal (horizontal) forgiveness and judicial/divine (vertical) forgiveness. The core biblical rule is that an individual can only release someone from the debt of an offence COMMITTED DIRECTLY AGAINST THEM. When a brother wrongs you, they have incurred a personal debt against you. You possess the spiritual and relational authority to cancel that specific debt. This is what Jesus addresses in Mt 18. If a person slanders you, steals from you, or wrongs you, you are commanded to forgive them so that bitterness does not defile you. However, your forgiveness only clears the horizontal ledger between you and that person; it does not clear the vertical standing before God’s eternal Law. They broke your law, not God’s Law. You can forgive anyone breaking your law, but you have no right to forgive the breaking of God’s Law. When a person sins, their offense is ultimately a violation of God’s holy law. Therefore, only God has the judicial authority to grant eternal, absolute absolution. In Mark 2:5, when Jesus told the sick of the palsy: "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee," the scribes accurately understood the theology of the OT when they reasoned in their hearts: "Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?" (Mark 2:7). The scribes’ premise was completely correct: only the offended party can forgive a debt, and since all sin is ultimately against God, only God can judicially wipe it away. They simply failed to realize that Jesus was God manifested in the flesh, possessing that very authority. In ROMAN CATHOLIC theology, the sacrament of Penance involves a priest hearing a confession and pronouncing judicial absolution ("I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit"). From a strict biblical perspective, this practice claims an authority that scripture never grants to a human mediator, neither the forgiveness of sins nor the use of the Trinitarian formula. When King David committed adultery with Bathsheba and murdered Uriah, he physically wronged human beings. Yet, when he repented in Psalm 51:4, he cried out to God: “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight..." (KJV). David understood that while his crimes had horizontal, earthly victims, the cosmic weight of his guilt was a vertical debt owed strictly to God. Uriah was dead and could not horizontally forgive him; Nathan the prophet could comfort David, but Nathan could not judicially absolve him. Only God could purge his sin. A third-party human cannot step in to arbitrate or dissolve a debt they did not experience. Catholics like to use John 20:23 as evidence of their authority to absolve sins: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained." (Jn 20:23 KJV). But the Biblical context does not support that interpretation, as none of the apostles went around telling individuals: “I absolve you” or “your sins are forgiven.” So, in order to better understand this verse, we need to realize that this is the Great Commission of Jesus as described by John. The other descriptions of the Great Commission are given by Matthew 28:19-20; Mark 16:15-18 & Luke 20:21-23. Let’s look at Luke’s account, since it’s the most similar to John’s. Both passages record the same post-resurrection appearance of Jessus to the assembled disciples on Easter Sunday evening. While John uses the terms “remit” and “retain”, Luke explicitly translates this mandate into the commission to preach the Gospel of repentance and remission of sins to all nations. John explains that Jesus “breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost” (Jn 20:22 KJV). Luke says that Jesus “opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Lk 24:45 KJV). By harmonizing both passages, we know that the receiving of the Holy Spirit here refers not to Spirit baptism (as that first happens in Acts 2), but to the opening of their minds to be able to understand. Then John continues to explain: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.” (Jn 20:23 KJV). While Luke describes this verse as: “And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem” (Lk 24:47 KJV). By harmonizing these two passages, we see that “remitting” or “retaining” sins refers to whether you preach the gospel of remission of sins or not. Jesus did not establish a judicial tribunal where individuals would kneel before an apostle to receive personal absolution. Instead, the authority to remit sins was tied directly to the proclamation of the message. Luke also specifies that this preaching must be done “in his name,” paralleling the singular name of the Father, Son,and Spirit by which the Great Commission was to be carried out in Matthew’s account (as explained by Mt 28:19). This also directly mirrors John 20:21 ("as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you"). The disciples have no intrinsic power to forgive sins; they operate strictly as ambassadors executing a decree under the authority of the singular King’s name of Jesus (YHWH-Saves). Jesus also gives a specific geographic anchor for this commission: “beginning at Jerusalem.” If we want to see exactly how the apostles understood the instructions they received in Mt 28:19-20, Mk 16:15-18; Lk 24:45-49 & Jn 20:21-23, we simply have to look at what they did when they arrived in Jerusalem. In Acts 2, when the Holy Ghost was poured out in Jerusalem, Peter DID NOT SET UP A CONFESSIONAL BOOTH. Instead, he stood up and PREACHED THE GOSPEL (Lk 24:47). When the convicted crowd asked, “Men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37), Peter executed John 20:23 and Luke 24:47 simultaneously by declaring the absolute terms of remission: "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." (Acts 2:38, KJV). By preaching repentance and baptism in the name of Jesus, Peter officially opened the door of “remission” to the three thousand who gladly received his word, while the sins of those who mocked remained “retained.” The modern Catholic practice is private auricular confession is a clear human development that was never taught neither by Jesus nor the apostles. For example, even that Catholic Catechism acknowledges that private auricular confession was developed by Irish monks in the 7th century: “During the seventh century Irish missionaries, inspired by the Eastern monastic tradition, took to continental Europe the "private" practice of penance, which does not require public and prolonged completion of penitential works before reconciliation with the Church. From that time on, the sacrament has been performed in secret between penitent and priest.” (CCC 1447). However, “privately” confessing your sins to your priest while sitting next to him led to many sexual scandals, so by the 16th century (in response to the Protestant Reformation) the Catholic Church decided to place their priests in Confessional Booths. Many historians acknowledge that they were implemented in response to “solicitation” (priests using confession to pursue inappropriate relationships or sexual advances), a problem addressed by post-Tridentine(after the Council of Trent) reforms. So if you want to be forgiven of your sins, the Bible is very explicit about how to do it: (1) “After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name… And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Mt 6:9,12 KJV). (2) "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 Jn 1:9 KJV); (3) David confesses directly to God: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." (Ps 32:5 KJV); (4) "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (Heb 4:16 KJV); (5) "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." (Mt 6:14 KJV) (6) The tax collector in Jesus’ parable sought forgiveness this way: "God be merciful to me a sinner." (Lk 18:13 KJV). Jesus said: "This man went down to his house justified rather than the other" (Lk 18:14 KJV); etc. THE ONLY THING NOT FOUND IN SCRIPTURE IS PRIVATE AURICULAR CONFESSION TO A ROMAN PRIEST.

23.x: Following Peter’s question about the limits of forgiveness. Jesus delivers the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (Mt 18:23-35). “Therefore..”: This connects the parable directly to the “seventy times seven” mandate in v.22. “... a certain king, which would take account…”: The king represents God. The settling of accounts indicates that human beings are fundamentally accountable to their Creator for their actions and spiritual debts.

24.x: “..which owed him ten thousand talents”: A single talent was worth roughly 6,000 denarii (a denarius being a day’s wage for a common laborer). Ten thousand talents equates to 60,000,000 days of labor: an astronomical, hyper-inflated sum meant to represent an absolutely unpayable debt. In Christ’s teaching, this illustrates the infinite weight of human sin against a holy God. We cannot work it off, buy it off, or live long enough to clear it.

25.x: “..commanded him to be sold…”: Under ancient laws, a bankrupt debtor and his family could be sold into bondservitude to liquidate assets. Yet, even selling the family would only recover a fraction of ten thousand talents. The servant is completely ruined.

26.x: “..I will pay thee all”: The servant’s plea is earnest but completely delusional. He is promising the impossible. He could never earn enough to pay back ten thousand talents. It reflects the mistake of trying to satisfy God through future human works or self-justification.

27.x: “..the lord of that servant was moved with compassion.. And forgave him the debt..”: The king does not grant an extension or a payment plan; he completely cancels the massive debt out of sheer compassion. This represents the total, unearned justification available through the grace of God.

28.x: “..the same servant.. Found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence..”: A hundred pence (denarii) is about 100 days of wages. While not pocket change, it is an entirely manageable, finite debt. “..took him by the throat..”: The staggering contrast is immediate. Fresh off being cleared of an unpayable fortune, the servant physically assaults a peer over a trivial sum.

29.x: “Have patience with me..”: The fellow-servant uses the exact same plea that the first servant used before the king.

30.x: Yet, the forgiven servant shows no mercy, demanding immediate legal vengeance and throwing his debtor into prison.

34.x: “..delivered him to the tormetors..”: The debt cancellation is revoked, and he is handed over to prison guards or jailers whose job was to ensure hard labor or punitive distress. “..till he should pay all..”: Because he can never pay back ten thousand talents, this “till” functions as an indicator of endless, permanent confinement.

35.x: “So likewise..”: Jesus applies the moral sharply. He is speaking directly to his disciples. If a believer harbors an unforgiving heart, they demonstrate that they have not truly internalized or submitted to God’s forgiveness, and they will face final, inescapable divine judgement. BEING ABLE TO FORGIVE OTHERS IS A SALVATION ISSUE.

Roman Catholicism teaches that this “prison” refers to Purgatory, which is defined as a place or state of temporal purification where those who die in God’s grace undergo cleansing for venial sins or satisfy the temporal punishment due to forgiven mortal sins before entering heaven. Catholics often point to the word “till” in v.34 to argue that the prison represents a temporary destination from which a soul can eventually be released once the debt is fully paid. However, Purgatory is not Biblical, and you can see how their argument quickly falls apart with a careful read of Scripture: (1) The impossibility of payment makes confinement PERMANENT. The entire premise of the parable relies on the fact that ten thousand talents is an unpayable amount. A standard prison sentence for a small debt could end when the debt was satisfied. But a debt of 100,000 lifetimes of labor can never be satisfied. Therefore, being delivered to the tormentors “till he should pay all” is a stylistic, idiomatic way of describing a sentence that never ends. It parallels the absolute finality of hell, not a temporary holding cell. (2) Purgatory applies to the justified; this man is re-condemned. According to Catholic dogma, only those who die in a state of grace (the saved) go to Purgatory. It is a place for God’s children to be refined. However, the servant in this passage is explicitly called “wicked” (v.32) and faces the fierce wrath of the King (“his lord ws wroth”, v.34). God does not send those who are under His saving grace to the “tormentors” in absolute fury. The language points to the final condemnation of an apostate or a hypocrite who has completely severed their relationship with the King. (3) Salvation is FREE, but purgatory implies self-payment. If the prison represents Purgatory where a soul suffers to satisfy its own remaining debt to God, it destroys the theological core of the parable. The parable teaches that the initial debt was totally, freely forgiven because the servant was entirely bankrupt (v.27). The servant was not thrown into prison to finish paying a balance; he was thrown into prison because his total pardon was completely revoked due to his malice. If a believer must go to a place of torment to pay off their own spiritual debt to God, then Christ’s sacrifice did not actually cancel the debt, and grace is no longer grace. (4) The structure of the parable parallels Final Judgement. Throughout Matthew’s Gospel, Jesus repeated uses the motif of being cast into an inescapable place of torment to describe Hell/Eternal Damnation, not a middle ground of purification. For example: Matthew 13:42 shows casting the wicked into a “furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.” In Matthew 22:13: “Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Also Matthew 25:46, where he says: “And these shall go away into everlasting punishment..”. So the phrase “delivered him to the tormentors” in Mt 18:34 matches this exact pattern of final, punitive retribution. There is no hint of refining, cleansing, or eventual restoration in the text; there is only enforcement of a massive, unpayable penalty upon a wicked, unforgiving heart.

31-33.x: “O thou wicked servant..”: The king’s disposition changes from compassion to severe judgement. The wicked servant’s fundamental failure was not the original debt, but his total refusal to allow the king’s mercy to transform how he treated others.
